walkthroughs.body_html: At an equinox the Sun lies on the celestial equator (Dec ~ 0). At the summer solstice the Sun reaches its highest declination (+23.5 degrees), giving the longest daylight in the northern hemisphere.

The Earth rotates once relative to the stars in ~23 h 56 min (sidereal day). Because Earth has also moved along its orbit, it takes ~4 extra minutes for the Sun to return to the same meridian — giving a 24 h solar day.
For 'explain why a star rises 4 minutes earlier each night': link sidereal vs solar day, Earth's orbital motion (~1 deg/day), and how this offsets star return times.

mcqs.q: Why don't we have a solar eclipse every new moon?
options: It moves backwards.
The Moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the Sun's apparent position.
Eclipses happen randomly.
Because clouds block them.

mcqs.q: Why was Pluto reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006?
options: Because the universe looks dark at night.
It is too small to be a planet.
It moves backwards.
It does not clear its orbital neighbourhood of similar-sized bodies.

mcqs.q: Why do astronomers infer the existence of dark matter?
options: Dark matter has been directly observed in telescopes.
Because the universe looks dark at night.
Visible matter alone cannot account for galaxy rotation curves and gravitational lensing.
Because clouds block them.
